name: Tiv
confidence_why: 2 independent first-hand descriptions agree (1 state the same rule, 0 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_citation: Angitso, Michael Terhemen. 2023. The enclitic in Tiv associative constructions and prepositional phrases. Nordic Journal of African Studies 32(1): 66-91. DOI 10.53228/njas.v32i1.807.
catalog_locator: Section 3 'Tonal behaviour in Tiv', journal pp. 68-69
catalog_quote: Basically, Tiv has two register tones, high [ ́] and low [ ̀] tones, abbreviated in the running text as H and L respectively. These two tones are lexically contrastive. Using the segmental base sule in (1), for example, a LL tone sequence yields the verb sùlè ‘to be deceased/cold’ and ... distinguishes it from other words, including words of other classes: sùlè ‘to be deceased/cold’ (LL) contrasts with the noun súlé ‘farm’ (HH), the noun súlè ‘coin’ (HL), and the verb sùlé ‘to cool’ (LH). ... Beyond lexical meaning and word class distinctions, variations in tone express morphological and grammatical contrasts such as noun class, as well as Tense, Aspect, and Mood (TAM) distinctions. ... The register tones interact transparently with prefixation and suffixation via the spreading and downdrift processes. The H tones in noun class prefixes spread onto the root nouns, elevating the pitch of lexical L tones to phonetic mid (henceforth, M), as in (3a), and sometimes elevating lexical H tones to extra H pitch levels, as in (3b).
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tiv is described as a two-tone (H/L) register-tone language with lexical and grammatical tone, contour tones HL/LH from floating tones, downdrift/downstep and a phonetic mid (Angitso 2022: 3; Angitso 2023: 68; Kaan & Yoo 2014: sec. 4.3, who also report Udu 2009's three-level H/M/L analysis). No opened source says anything about where word stress falls; the only stress-related remark is Aor (2021: 1), who calls Tiv 'a syllable-timed language' in contrast with stress-timed English.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None: no source discusses stress at all. Aor 2021 (JLLLS 1(1): 1, file): 'English, a stress-timed language, has loaned out a lot of lexical items to Tiv, a syllable-timed language that is spoken in the north-central geographical zone of Nigeria and the Republic of Cameroon.'
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone (nouns and verbs, citation and phrasal contexts); the tone descriptions concern lexical tone and tonal morphology, not prominence. The full grammars (Abraham 1940, Jockers 1991, Willemsen 2014) that might contain a remark on stress/emphasis could not be opened.
new_statements.identity_note: All opened sources describe Tiv of Benue State, Nigeria (Angitso: Hamburg-based description of Nigerian Tiv; Kaan & Yoo, Aor, Ugechi & Ayagah, Udu: Benue State University / NINLAN authors); Willemsen's unseen sketch is based on a Makurdi speaker and Kenen & Yonou 2024 on the Gboko lect. Glottolog tivv1240 lists no dialect-level glottocodes; no separately named variety is at issue.

new_statements.quote: The lack of consistency in stress patterns of two-syllable words among the speakers indicates the complex interplay between their native tonal language and the stress patterns of English. [...] Considering the tension between pitch and duration in determining primary stress in TivE, it is noteworthy that the variety has tonal backgrounds where the pitch of a syllable carries lexical or grammatical meaning, but the duration may play a relatively insignificant role in determining stress patterns.

Quote part 2 is verbatim at lines 555-558 on the page with printed footer '13' (form feeds 548-600), under '4.3 Statistical Discussion' (line 527): 'Considering the tension between pitch and duration in determining primary stress in TivE, it is noteworthy that the variety has tonal backgrounds…
new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the existing Angitso 2023 statement that Tiv is a tone language with no word-stress rule stated, but only incidentally: the work describes Tiv-English (a sub-variety of Nigerian English) and characterises the speakers' L1 as 'their native tonal language' / a language with 'tonal backgrounds where the pitch of a syllable carries lexical or grammatical meaning'. It is not a phonological description of Tiv and should not be cited as a Tiv stress source; it neither confirms nor denies a Tiv word-stress rule.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The paper's object is Tiv-English (the English of Tiv bilinguals), not Tiv. About Tiv itself it says only that it is a tonal language in which syllable pitch carries lexical or grammatical meaning; it gives no rule for Tiv word stress. Its stress findings (e.g. 84.5% of isolated-word placements matching other Nigerian English varieties; constraint ranking NSR>>ROOTING>>LHR>>RHR) concern English words.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing for Tiv; secondary stress is not discussed even for Tiv-English.
new_statements.identity_note: Amoniyan 2023 describes Tiv-English, the L2 English of Tiv bilinguals (50 respondents from the Federal University of Agriculture Makurdi and Benue State University, from different parts of Benue State); it loosely calls Tiv 'the Tiv dialect'. Its statements about stress are about English words, not Tiv; only the two quoted sentences bear on Tiv (as a tonal L1). No Tiv dialect is singled out.

tone_statements.citation: Tyonyion, Terdoo Joseph. 2026. A contrastive study of tone and intonation as prosodic features in Tiv and English phonology. American Journal of Multifunctional Publishing 3(7): 368-379. ISSN 2997-3287. DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21533738
tone_statements.quote: Tiv language has been viewed primarily as a tonal language while English is viewed as a stress timed language. In tonal languages, tones can therefore be properly tone marked so as to identify both the lexical and grammatical functions of tones in the phonological structure, which Tiv language is a typical example. [...] In Tiv language, tone marks also identify tenses and plural forms. (p. 375) / In Tiv the intonation pattern is what is described as down-drift which means a high tone after a low tone is lower than the preceding high tone and a low tone after a high tone can also be lower than the preceding lower tone. (p. 373)

tone_statements.citation: Usar, Ignatius Iornenge. 2025. Verb tone in Tiv: a focus on tense and aspect. International Journal of Language, Linguistics, Literature and Culture 4(6): 21-39. DOI 10.59009/ijlllc.2025.0158
tone_statements.quote: Tiv exhibits a tonal inventory of three phonemic-level tones - High (H), Mid (M), and Low (L), as well as contour tones such as rising and falling. These tonal distinctions are not merely phonetic but are structurally encoded into the language's grammar. Processes such as tone spreading, tone doubling, and downstep further complicate the tonal landscape, contributing to the complex realisation of verbal forms (Pulleyblank, 1988; Arnott, 1964).
tone_statements.locator: p. 21, section 1 Introduction; see also p. 25 below Table 1 and section 4.3 'Downstep as a Feature of Verbal Inflection' pp. 29-32
tone_statements.summary: Author's analysis: 3 level tones H/M/L + rising and falling contours; downstep (!H from floating L); grammatical tone on verbs for tense/aspect/mood; tone spreading.

tone_statements.citation: Karshima, Daniel T. 2012 [revised and reprinted 2014]. Comprehensive Tiv Orthography. Makurdi: Doo-Ter Books Publications. ISBN 978-978-923-355-7. 50 pp. (Chapter 5 'Tone marking', pp. 44-49.)
tone_statements.quote: Take a look at this word ‘tor’ which has four different sounds to differentiate the meanings from each other. ... ‘tor’ – king (mid tone). ‘tőr’ – pestle (high tone). ‘tór’ – to push something into another with force (mid-high tone). ‘tǒr’ – thatched grass (low-high tone). Ordinarily written, there is no difference between each of the words, only the tones that keep changing. It is observed that the first ‘tor’ is not marked because it is a plain (mid tone). The second is high-high. The third is mid-high and the fourth is high-low.
tone_statements.summary: Orthography guide, no toneme count: high, mid (unmarked), low levels plus mid-high/low-high/high-low shapes; 4th 'tor' labelled both low-high and high-low. P. 10 calls Tiv 'a tonal language'.

tone_statements.quote: Im Subjunktiv 1° sind die Téne alle tief. Der Ton hat also hier, von Klasse 2 abgesehen, grammatische Funktion. ... kann man allgemein sagen, daB sie meist tieftonig vor einem folgenden Hochton sind. Sie kénnen aber alle Mittelton annehmen, und zwar tritt dies vor folgendem Tiefton ein ... Endet der Nominal- stamm auf einen Konsonanten und ist er tieftonig, dann verursacht der Hochton einen steigenden Ton
tone_statements.translation: In the subjunctive the tones are all low. Tone thus has grammatical function here, apart from class 2. ... one can say in general that they [the stable genitive particles] are mostly low-toned before a following high tone. But they can all take mid tone, and this happens before a following low tone ... If the noun stem ends in a consonant and is low-toned, the high tone causes a rising tone
tone_statements.summary: H/M/L level terms used throughout; rising, falling and an H-to-M 'compound' tone arise in genitive sandhi; no count stated. All data are Abraham's 1940 notations.
